data.title: Incontinentia pigmenti — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Incontinentia pigmenti** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is incontinentia pigmenti (IP, Bloch–Sulzberger)?**
- X-linked dominant multisystem genodermatosis due to IKBKG (NEMO) mutations (commonly exon 4–10 deletion) — lethal in males in utero (affected females; rare males with Klinefelter or mosaicism); skewed X-inactivation
- Defective NF-κB activation → keratinocyte apoptosis and inflammation along Blaschko's lines

**Q2. Describe the stages.**
- Stage 1 — vesicular/inflammatory (birth–4 months): linear vesicles and bullae on erythematous base along Blaschko's lines on limbs/trunk, with blood eosinophilia
- Stage 2 — verrucous (2–6 months): linear warty keratotic plaques (limbs)
- Stage 3 — hyperpigmented (6 months–adolescence): swirling/whorled slate-grey to brown pigmentation along Blaschko's lines on trunk (not necessarily at earlier sites)
- Stage 4 — hypopigmented/atrophic (adolescence/adult): pale, hairless, anhidrotic linear streaks on calves
- Stages may overlap or be absent

**Q3. Extracutaneous features.**
- Teeth (most common extracutaneous ~80%): hypodontia/anodontia, conical/peg teeth, delayed eruption
- Hair: vertex scarring alopecia, woolly hair; nails: dystrophy, painful subungual keratotic tumours (later life)
- Eyes (~35%): retinal vasculopathy, retinal detachment, strabismus, microphthalmia — urgent ophthalmology review and serial retinal exams in infancy
- CNS (~30%): seizures, intellectual disability, spastic paresis, microcephaly, stroke-like lesions
- Breast hypoplasia, supernumerary nipples

**Q4. Histopathology by stage.**
- Stage 1: eosinophilic spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles full of eosinophils, dyskeratotic cells
- Stage 2: hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, dyskeratosis (whorls)
- Stage 3: marked pigment incontinence (dermal melanophages) — origin of the name
- Stage 4: atrophic epidermis, absent adnexa

**Q5. Diagnostic criteria (Minić et al. 2014).**
- Major: typical skin lesions at any stage along Blaschko's lines
- Minor: dental, ocular, CNS anomalies, alopecia/woolly hair, nail abnormalities, palate anomalies, breast/nipple anomalies, multiple male miscarriages, typical histology
- With positive IKBKG mutation, any one major or minor criterion suffices

**Q6. Differential diagnosis (stage-wise).**
- Stage 1: bullous impetigo, HSV, varicella, EB, bullous mastocytosis, LCH
- Stage 2: linear epidermal naevus, warts, lichen striatus
- Stage 3: linear and whorled naevoid hypermelanosis (no preceding stages), X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Naegeli syndrome
- Stage 4: hypomelanosis of Ito, Goltz syndrome, linear morphoea

**Q7. Management.**
- Skin: supportive, gentle wound care, prevent infection — lesions resolve spontaneously
- Multidisciplinary follow-up: ophthalmology (retinal exam at diagnosis and frequently in first year; laser photocoagulation), neurology (MRI if neurological signs), dental care, developmental assessment
- Genetic counselling: 50% risk to daughters; affected male pregnancies usually miscarry

**Q8. Describe the four stages in detail.**
- Stage 1 (vesicular, birth–4 months): linear vesicles/ pustules on erythematous base along Blaschko lines, eosinophilia
- Stage 2 (verrucous, weeks–months): warty hyperkeratotic linear plaques mostly on limbs
- Stage 3 (hyperpigmented, months–adolescence): swirling grey-brown streaks/ whorls on trunk (not necessarily same sites)
- Stage 4 (atrophic/ hypopigmented, adolescence–adulthood): hairless, anhidrotic pale atrophic streaks on legs
- Stages may overlap or be skipped

**Q9. Histopathology by stage in detail.**
- Stage 1: eosinophilic spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles full of eosinophils
- Stage 2: hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, dyskeratotic cells in whorls
- Stage 3: pigment incontinence — melanophages in dermis
- Stage 4: atrophic epidermis, absent adnexa

**Q10. Differential diagnosis of vesicular stage.**
- Neonatal HSV infection (critical — do Tzanck/ PCR), bullous impetigo, epidermolysis bullosa, varicella, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, transient neonatal pustular melanosis, linear IgA disease

**Q11. Management and follow-up.**
- Wound care for vesicles (avoid infection), skin lesions resolve; genetic testing (IKBKG deletion); urgent ophthalmology screening (retinal vasculopathy — laser), neurological assessment and MRI if symptomatic, dental review (implants), genetic counselling (50% risk to daughters; male pregnancies often miscarry)

**Q12. What is NEMO and its other disorders?**
- NF-κB essential modulator (IKKγ) — required for NF-κB activation (protects cells from TNF-induced apoptosis); hypomorphic IKBKG mutations in males cause anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency (EDA-ID)

**Q13. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q14. Explain the genetics and why it is mostly female.**
- X-linked dominant IKBKG (NEMO) mutation — commonest a recurrent exon 4–10 deletion; usually lethal in hemizygous males (in utero), so mostly girls; affected males survive with Klinefelter (XXY) or somatic mosaicism; extreme skewed X-inactivation in carrier mothers

**Q15. Dental, hair and nail changes.**
- Teeth: hypodontia/anodontia, conical/peg-shaped teeth, delayed eruption (most common extracutaneous feature)
- Hair: vertex scarring alopecia (cicatricial), woolly hair, sparse eyebrows
- Nails: dystrophy, painful subungual keratotic tumours in adolescence/adulthood (may erode bone — mimic SCC)

**Q16. What eye and CNS findings are critical?**
- Retinal vascular abnormalities (peripheral avascularity, neovascularisation) → retinal detachment and blindness — needs ophthalmology screening from birth (monthly early, then periodically) and laser photocoagulation
- CNS: seizures, ischaemic strokes, developmental delay, spastic paralysis — in ~30%; neonatal encephalopathy

## Quick spotter facts
- Female infant with linear vesicles along Blaschko's lines + eosinophilia — IP stage 1 (NEMO)
- Peg teeth, retinal vasculopathy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Incontinentia pigmenti). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
